name: Isoxsuprine
lead: Isoxsuprine is a beta-adrenergic agonist and peripheral vasodilator that relaxes vascular and uterine smooth muscle [1]. It has been used in people for circulation problems and to slow premature labour, and in horses for hoof conditions such as navicular disease and laminitis [1][2].

Its place in appearance discussions comes from its beta-agonist class. Beta-adrenergic stimulation raises circulating free fatty acids, and people interested in leaner physiques ask whether related drugs could contribute to fat loss. The chain is a claimed one: beta stimulation, more free fatty acids available as fuel, a leaner look. Physiology work on adrenergic-stimulating agents examined how they change plasma growth hormone, insulin and free fatty acid levels [11]; research on isoxsuprine itself has focused on circulation and uterine uses.

Published studies include a Cochrane review of beta2-agonists for period pain, randomised trials in oral submucous fibrosis and vasculogenic impotence, and a trial in navicular disease in horses [3][4][5][6]. It is a prescription drug, and Grokipedia reports that US approval of its oral products was withdrawn in 2020 [2].

angle.text: Isoxsuprine is a vasodilator and beta agonist, and people interested in leaner physiques discuss it because of that beta-agonist class. Its documented uses are circulatory and obstetric.

infobox: Prescription drug; US approval withdrawn 2020 per Grokipedia [2]

paras: Isoxsuprine has the formula C18H23NO3 and a molar mass of about 301 g/mol. It is a phenylethanolamine derivative, usually supplied as the hydrochloride salt [1].

In people, isoxsuprine has been used as a vasodilator in conditions such as Raynaud's phenomenon and cerebral vascular insufficiency, and as a tocolytic for preterm labour [1][7][8]. A 1974 clinical trial examined it as an oral vasodilator [9]. A 1975 trial examined it in primary dysmenorrhoea and premenstrual tension [15].

In horses it is used for hoof problems including navicular disease and laminitis, based on the idea that it improves hoof circulation; Wikipedia notes it is given orally and should not be used in bleeding horses or mares just after foaling [1]. A double-blind study evaluated it for navicular disease [10]. It is a prohibited class B substance under FEI competition rules and is often banned by other equine organisations; it can remain detectable in urine for weeks or months [1].

The interest in isoxsuprine among people pursuing leanness is theoretical and drawn from its class. It is sometimes grouped with other beta agonists discussed for fat loss. No published study has measured its effect on body fat, and its documented uses remain circulatory and obstetric [1][2].

Isoxsuprine acts as a beta2-adrenergic agonist, relaxing smooth muscle directly [1]. Earlier physiology work examined how adrenergic-blocking or stimulating agents change plasma growth hormone, insulin and free fatty acid levels in people [11].

Wikipedia reports oral bioavailability of about 100 percent in humans versus about 2.2 percent in horses, an onset of around one hour, an elimination half-life under three hours in horses, and mainly renal excretion [1].

Reported effects include dizziness, flushing, faster heart rate, low blood pressure, nausea and nervousness; it may also irritate the gastrointestinal tract, and caution is advised with other blood-pressure-affecting drugs such as sedatives and anesthetics [1][2].

Grokipedia reports US FDA approval in 1959 under the brand Vasodilan and a Drug Efficacy Study Implementation review that led to withdrawal of approval of oral products in 2020 [2]. Early obstetric reports date to the 1960s [12], and reviews of preterm-labour therapy in 1983 discussed it among tocolytics [8].
Brand names include Vasodilan and Duvadilan [1]. It is generally prescription-only [1]. Its status as a prohibited substance in equestrian competition is part of its profile outside medicine [1].

A Cochrane review found trials of beta2-agonists, including oral isoxsuprine, for primary dysmenorrhoea [3]. A randomised trial in 40 people with oral submucous fibrosis compared isoxsuprine with dexamethasone and hyaluronidase injections [4]. A randomised crossover study compared yohimbine plus isoxsuprine with pentoxifylline in vasculogenic impotence [5]. A 2022 study compared oral nifedipine with parenteral isoxsuprine for arresting preterm labour [13]. A small phase 1/2 trial tested isoxsuprine in multiple sclerosis relapses [14]. A 2024 sheep study did not find increased fertility after artificial insemination with isoxsuprine [16]. No studies on isoxsuprine for body-fat reduction were found.

card.note: Prescription vasodilator; can lower blood pressure and raise heart rate.

quick.overview:
Isoxsuprine is a prescription vasodilator and beta2 agonist. It has been used for circulation problems, for slowing premature labour, and in horses for hoof conditions.

In appearance circles it comes up as a beta agonist that people connect with fat loss, though its documented uses are circulatory and obstetric.
quick.mechanism: It stimulates beta2-adrenergic receptors, relaxing the smooth muscle of blood vessels and the uterus. Beta stimulation in general raises circulating free fatty acids, which is the basis of the fat-loss interest.
quick.risks: Reported effects include dizziness, flushing, fast heart rate, low blood pressure and nausea. It is a prescription drug, and Grokipedia reports US approval of its products was withdrawn in 2020.
